title: Octopuses Can Use Mirrors to Find Hidden Snacks!
summary: Have you ever used a mirror to see something behind you? Maybe to check your hair or see who's sneaking up on you. Well, guess what? Octopuses can do that too! Scientists at Dartmouth College taught octopuses to use mirrors to find hidden food. That's a big deal because only some mammals and birds were known to do this before. The researchers worked with three California two-spot octopuses. First, they let the octopuses get used to a mirror in their tank. Then they showed them a virtual crab on a screen, but the octopus could only see it in the mirror. To get a real crab treat, the octopus had to turn around and go to the right spot. At first, the octopuses were a bit confused. But soon they figured it out. They got faster and faster at finding the treat. Some even climbed over the side of their box to get there quicker! Why is this so cool? Octopuses are very different from us. Our last common ancestor was a worm that lived hundreds of millions of years ago. Yet they evolved a similar skill. This helps scientists understand how intelligence can develop in different animals. Octopuses hunt in tricky places like coral reefs. Using a mirror might help them build a mental map of their surroundings. So next time you see an octopus, remember: they might be smarter than your reflection!
why_it_matters: Learning about smart animals like octopuses might help us understand how we think and invent new ways to solve problems.

background_read: Scientists once thought using mirrors to see hidden things was a skill only some mammals, like dolphins and apes, and some birds had.
This new discovery shows that octopuses, which are related to clams and snails, can do it too.

The study happened at Dartmouth College (a university in the United States), where researchers tested three California two-spot octopuses (a type of octopus that lives along the coast of California and Mexico).
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at Dartmouth College and three California two-spot octopuses
WHAT: Taught octopuses to use a mirror to find hidden food treats
WHERE: In a tank at the researchers' laboratory
WHY: To understand how intelligence can develop in very different animals, like octopuses that are far from humans on the tree of life

perspectives.description: This discovery is exciting because it shows that octopuses are much smarter than we once thought, and it may lead to more research on animal intelligence.
Some scientists might argue that the octopuses were just learning a trick for a treat, and it doesn't prove they understand mirrors like humans do.
The study is small—only three octopuses—so more research is needed to see if this skill is common among all octopuses or just these individuals.
